examples.problem_statement: Which quadrants, if any, do not contain any points on the line represented by x - y = 18 ?

solution.description: Rewrite the given equation in slope-intercept form by solving for y, so the line's slope and y-intercept are visible.
Set x = 0 in the rewritten equation to find the y-intercept of the line.
Set y = 0 in the same equation to find the x-intercept of the line.

solution.operation: \text{plot } (0, -18) \text{ and } (18, 0), \text{ draw the line through them}
solution.result: a line rising through the fourth, first and third quadrants
solution.description: Plot the two intercepts on the coordinate plane and draw the line joining them, so you can see which regions it sweeps through.

solution.operation: \text{read off the quadrant the drawn line never enters}
solution.description: Inspect the drawn line and identify the quadrant it does not pass through.

key_reminders: Solving a linear equation for y puts it in slope-intercept form y = mx + b.
Setting x = 0 gives the y-intercept; setting y = 0 gives the x-intercept.
Two plotted points determine the line, and the drawn line shows which quadrants it occupies.
common_mistakes: Rearranging x - y = 18 as y = 18 - x (sign error on y), which flips the slope and points at the wrong empty quadrant.
Swapping the intercepts and plotting (-18, 0) and (0, 18) instead of (0, -18) and (18, 0).

concept.technique_name: Pythagorean triple plus rectangle area equality

examples.problem_statement: Rectangles ABCD and EFGH have equal areas. In the figure, right triangle ACD has hypotenuse AC = 10 and leg AD = 8, and rectangle EFGH has side EF = 12. What is the length of side FG?

solution.description: Use the right triangle ACD, whose two known sides make it a 6-8-10 Pythagorean triple (or apply the Pythagorean Theorem), to get the missing side CD.
Multiply the length AD by the width CD to get the area of rectangle ABCD.
Transfer the area you just computed to rectangle EFGH, since the problem states the two rectangles have equal areas.
Write the area of EFGH as its known side EF times the unknown side FG, setting it equal to 48.
Divide both sides by 12 to solve the equation for FG.

key_reminders: A right triangle with a leg of 8 and hypotenuse 10 is the 6-8-10 Pythagorean triple.
Area of a rectangle = length x width.
Equal areas let you carry a computed area from one figure straight into the other.
common_mistakes: Treating 10 as a leg and computing CD from 8 and 10 as legs instead of recognizing 10 as the hypotenuse.
Dividing 48 by 6 or 8 instead of by the given side EF = 12 when solving for FG.

examples.problem_statement: If your stock portfolio increased by 25% and then decreased by 20%, what percent of the original value would your new stock portfolio have?

solution.description: Since no real starting amount is given, pick $100 as the original value of the portfolio.
Apply the 25% increase to the picked value: it grows by $25 to a new value of $125.
Apply the 20% decrease by multiplying the new value by 0.8, since dropping 20% is the same as keeping 80%.
Compare the final value to the value you started with to express the result as a percent of the original.
Check the same result algebraically by multiplying the two successive percent multipliers, which come to exactly 1.

key_reminders: When no real amount is specified in a percent problem, pick 100 for the starting value.
A decrease of 20% means multiplying by 100% - 20% = 80%, i.e. 0.8.
Successive percent changes multiply: Original x 1.25 x 0.80 = New.
common_mistakes: Adding and subtracting the percents (25% - 20% = 5%) instead of applying them successively.
Taking the 20% decrease off the original 100 rather than off the new value of 125.

concept.technique_name: locating a median by cumulative percent in grouped data
concept.sub_category: circle graph - median of grouped data

examples.problem_statement:
A circle graph separates 10 million unemployed manufacturing industry workers into five groups by length of unemployment in weeks, giving the percent of workers in each group: the 1-to-4 week group holds 40% of the workers and the next group, 5 to 10 weeks, holds 20%. Which of the following could be the median length of unemployment, in weeks, for manufacturing industry workers who were unemployed for at least 1 week?
(A) 4  (B) 8  (C) 12  (D) 16  (E) 20

solution.operation: 10{,}000{,}000 \text{ lengths, one per worker, grouped into five intervals with given percents}
solution.result: an ordered list of 10 million whole-number week lengths
solution.description: Read the circle graph as one unemployment length per worker, so the five sectors describe how 10 million rounded whole-number lengths split across the intervals.

solution.operation: \text{median} = \text{value at which } 50\% \text{ of the ordered lengths have been listed}
solution.description: Restate the median as the middle of the ordered list, that is, the point where 50% of the lengths have already been listed.
Start the ordered list with the shortest group, 1 to 4 weeks, which accounts for the first 40% of the lengths.

solution.result: the 50\% mark falls inside the 5-to-10 week group
solution.description: Add the next group, 5 to 10 weeks at 20%, which carries the cumulative count past the 50% mark, so the median sits in that interval.
Test each answer choice against the 5-to-10 week interval and keep the only one that lies inside it.

key_reminders: The median is the value at which 50% of the ordered data has been listed.
With grouped data you only need cumulative percents, not the individual values, to locate which interval contains the median.
Percents in a circle graph can be accumulated in order from the smallest interval upward.
common_mistakes: Choosing 4, the top of the 40% group, by stopping at the largest interval before the 50% mark is reached.
Averaging the interval midpoints or the answer choices instead of tracking the cumulative percent to 50%.
